problems.problem:
A. A twenty-franc arithmetic warm-up

The design of the Swiss 20-franc banknote of 2017 is inspired by light. Distances in light seconds (symbol ls, from the English *light second*) between the Earth and various celestial bodies are written in small print on the banknote.

a) The banknote gives the distance between the Earth and the Sun as 494 ls. What distance $r$ in kilometres and in astronomical units does this correspond to? [1 point]

The Earth's orbit around the Sun is elliptical with a low eccentricity. In the following few parts we will try to find out to which day of the year this distance approximately corresponds.

b) Compute the true anomaly $\nu$, the eccentric anomaly $E$ and the mean anomaly $M$ of the Earth corresponding to the distance $r$ computed in part a). Give the results numerically in degrees. [6 points]

c) The Earth passes perihelion on 4 January. Which day of the year can correspond to the distance written on the 20-franc banknote? [3 points]

Figure 1: The true anomaly $\nu$ and the eccentric anomaly $E$ marked on the orbital ellipse. The planet is marked by a black dot. The Sun is at the focus $F_1$.

Hint: The true anomaly is the angle between the planet, the Sun and the perihelion. The eccentric anomaly is defined using a circle of radius equal to the semi-major axis of the ellipse, centred at the centre of the ellipse. If we draw through the planet a perpendicular to the axis of the ellipse, then the angle between the intersection of the perpendicular with the circle, the centre of the circle and the perihelion is the eccentric anomaly. See Figure 1. The mean anomaly is the angle that the planet would cover on the circle in the time since perihelion passage if it moved with a uniform angular velocity with the same total orbital period. Between the semi-major axis $a$ and the eccentricity $e$ of the orbit, the true anomaly $\nu$ and the distance from the Sun $r$ there is the relation
$$r = \frac{a(1-e^2)}{1+e\cos\nu}.$$
Between the true anomaly $\nu$ and the eccentric anomaly $E$ there is the relation
$$\tan\frac{\nu}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}}\,\tan\frac{E}{2}.$$
Between the eccentric anomaly $E$ and the mean anomaly $M$ the relation
$$M = E - e\sin E$$
holds. Between the mean anomaly $M$, the orbital period of the planet $T$ and the time since perihelion passage $t$ the relation
$$M = \frac{2\pi t}{T}$$
holds.

B. Contraction

Before the atomic nucleus and the equivalence of mass and energy were known, Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz proposed that the Sun shines because it is contracting as a whole. Estimate to an order of magnitude the time $t_{\mathrm{KH}}$ (numerically in years) for which the Sun could shine at its present power thanks to the energy gained from gravitational contraction. Give arguments why this mechanism cannot be the right one. In which phase of its evolution was gravitational contraction a relevant source of energy for the Sun?

C. The treacherous lamp

Kuba likes photographing the night sky from his balcony ($\varphi = 50.09^\circ$ N, $\lambda = 14.42^\circ$ E). His observations are, however, spoilt by a lit lamp with horizontal coordinates $h_L = 30^\circ$ (altitude above the horizon) and $A_L = 111^\circ$ (azimuth, measured in the standard way from north towards east). In what range of declinations can Kuba not take photographs if he wants to ensure a minimum distance of $10^\circ$ of the photographed object from the lamp at any time and on any day of the year?

D. Occultation of Neptune at opposition

An observer on the Earth watches an occultation of Neptune by an asteroid at opposition. Assume that the orbits of the asteroid and of Neptune lie in the plane of the ecliptic. The asteroid has diameter $D_p = (1.8 \pm 0.3)$ km and orbits the Sun on a circular orbit of radius $a_p = (2.24 \pm 0.18)$ au. Neptune has diameter $D_N = 49\,530$ km and at opposition it is at distance $r_N = 29.07$ au from the Earth. Assume that the occultation is central, i.e. that at the middle of the occultation the observer lies on one straight line with the centre of the asteroid and of Neptune's disc. Determine the total duration $T$ of the occultation (from first to last contact) and its uncertainty. Write the results numerically in seconds. At the moment of the observation the Earth is at distance $a_Z = 1.00$ au from the Sun.

Hint: The relative uncertainty of the $n$-th power of a quantity is $|n|$ times the relative uncertainty of that quantity.

E. Radio Saturn

In this problem you will estimate the monochromatic radiant flux $\Phi_\nu$ at the frequency $\nu = 300$ GHz that we record on the Earth as a result of the thermal radiation of Saturn's rings. Also assume that the dust particles have, at the given frequency, a Bond albedo $A_{\mathrm{B}} = 0.5$ and that the ring is thin enough to be as a whole in thermodynamic equilibrium. We are interested only in the thermal radiation emitted by the dust in the ring; do not consider reflected (scattered) radiation. Throughout the problem assume that we observe at the moment when the distance of Saturn from the Earth reaches its minimum value $d = 8$ au.

Figure 3: Saturn in the millimetre band. The figure is given for illustration and is not needed to solve the problem.

a) Compute the temperature $T$ (numerically in K) at which the dust particles in Saturn's ring settle. [2.5 points]

The equation of radiative transfer says that on passing through a layer of medium of thickness $\Delta s$ the monochromatic intensity $I_\nu$ of radiation (the quantity giving the emitted spectral radiant flux density per unit solid angle covered by the source) changes by
$$\Delta I_\nu = \left(\frac{j_\nu}{\kappa_\nu} - I_\nu\right)\varrho\,\kappa_\nu\,\Delta s\,, \qquad (3)$$
where $j_\nu$ is the emission coefficient per unit mass of the medium and $\varrho$ is the density of the medium. Throughout the problem we assume that the dust in the rings is in local thermodynamic equilibrium. Kirchhoff's law therefore holds in the form
$$\frac{j_\nu}{\kappa_\nu} = B_\nu \approx \frac{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\nu^2}{c^2}\,, \qquad (4)$$
where $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and we have approximated the Planck function $B_\nu$ by the Rayleigh–Jeans law.

We shall first assume that the medium of the ring is optically thin, i.e. that the energy radiated by the dust particles in the ring is not absorbed in the ring itself. This means that we neglect the second (absorption) term on the right-hand side of the radiative transfer equation (3). Under this assumption the radiative transfer equation reduces to the form
$$\Delta I_{\nu,\mathrm{thin}} = B_\nu\,\varrho\,\kappa_\nu\,\Delta s = \frac{2k_{\mathrm{B}}T\nu^2}{c^2}\,\varrho\,\kappa_\nu\,\Delta s\,. \qquad (5)$$
We shall consider the quantities $\varrho$, $\kappa_\nu$ and $T$ to be constant across the cross-section of the ring.

b) Write the general relation for the monochromatic intensity $I_{\nu,\mathrm{thin}}$ of the thermal radiation emitted in the direction perpendicular to the ring under the assumption of the optically thin regime. Express the result in terms of $k_{\mathrm{B}}$, $T$, $\nu$, $c$, $\varrho$, $\kappa_\nu$ and the thickness $D$ of the ring. [1 point]

The monochromatic intensity $I_\nu$ can in general be converted into the observed monochromatic radiant flux $\Phi_\nu$ (power incident per unit area at the given frequency) using the relation
$$\Phi_\nu \approx I_\nu\,\Delta\Omega\,,$$
where $\Delta\Omega$ is the solid angle (in steradians) that the source covers on the sky. We consider $\Delta\Omega \ll 1$.

Assume that the total mass of the dust component of the ring that contributes most to the observed radiation is $2.1\cdot10^{17}$ kg. At the given frequency $\nu = 300$ GHz this dust has the monochromatic opacity $\kappa_\nu = 1\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$.

c) Compute the monochromatic flux $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{thin}}$ from the whole ring observed from the Earth under the assumption of the optically thin regime. Explain thoroughly why in the optically thin case the resulting flux is independent of the inclination of the plane of the rings to the observer. Give the result generally in terms of $M$, $\kappa_\nu$, $k_{\mathrm{B}}$, $T$, $\nu$, $d$, $c$ and numerically in janskys, where $1\ \mathrm{Jy} = 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,Hz^{-1}}$. [3 points]

Now let us try to model Saturn's rings as an optically thick radiator. In such a regime, on passing through a layer $\Delta s$ of the ring medium there is an equilibrium between emitted and absorbed radiation, i.e. $\Delta I_\nu = 0$. From the right-hand side of the radiative transfer equation (3) and Kirchhoff's law (4) it then follows that we set the monochromatic intensity emitted by the surface of the ring directly equal to the Planck function, i.e.
$$I_{\nu,\mathrm{thick}} = B_\nu\,. \qquad (6)$$
For $B_\nu$ we shall continue to use the Rayleigh–Jeans approximation. In the following tasks consider the inner radius of the rings $R_{\mathrm{in}} = 67\,000$ km, the outer radius $R_{\mathrm{out}} = 140\,000$ km and the inclination $i = 27^\circ$ of the plane of the rings to the ecliptic.

d) Assuming the optically thick regime, compute the maximum value of the monochromatic flux $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{thick}}$ that we can observe from Saturn in the course of time. Give the result generally in terms of $k_{\mathrm{B}}$, $T$, $\nu$, $d$, $c$, $R_{\mathrm{in}}$, $R_{\mathrm{out}}$, $i$ and numerically in Jy. [3 points]

Let us now try to decide which of the two regimes considered above is actually realised. The criterion can be formulated using the dimensionless optical depth
$$\tau = \varrho\,\kappa_\nu\,\Delta s\,, \qquad (7)$$
belonging to the path $\Delta s$ that the radiation has travelled in the medium of the ring. If $\tau$ satisfies $\tau \ll 1$, the medium is optically thin; in the case $\tau \gg 1$, on the contrary, we have the optically thick regime.

e) Determine the minimum optical depth $\tau_{\min}$ of Saturn's ring observed from the Earth in the course of time. Express the result generally in terms of the fluxes $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{thin}}$ and $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{thick}}$ that you obtained in parts c) and d). Also write the numerical value of $\tau_{\min}$. [2.5 points]

On the basis of your results you should conclude that, as seen from the Earth, the optically thin regime never occurs. Moreover, the configuration considered in part e) (minimum observed optical depth) corresponds neither to the optically thin nor to the optically thick regime, since $\tau$ came out of the order of a few units.

For general values of $\tau$, interpolating between the optically thin and optically thick regimes, we must integrate the radiative transfer equation (3). We would then obtain the correct relation
$$I_\nu(\tau) = B_\nu\left(1 - e^{-\tau}\right) \qquad (8)$$
for the monochromatic intensity $I_\nu(\tau)$ emitted by the ring towards the observer as a function of the optical depth $\tau$ of the ring along the ray.

f) Show that for $\tau \ll 1$, resp. $\tau \gg 1$, relation (8) indeed gives the result for the intensity $I_{\nu,\mathrm{thin}}$ in the optically thin regime derived in part b), resp. relation (6) for the intensity $I_{\nu,\mathrm{thick}}$ in the optically thick regime. [1.5 points]

Hint: The approximate relation $e^x \approx 1 + x$, valid for $x \ll 1$, may be useful.

g) Compute the actual maximum value of the monochromatic flux $\Phi_\nu$ of the thermal radiation of Saturn's rings (numerically in Jy) that we can measure on the Earth in the course of time. Compare with the results of parts c) and d). [3 points]

Hint: The function $f(x) = (1 - e^{-x})/x$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x \in \langle 0, \infty)$.

In the last part of the problem we look at the radio radiation coming from the disc of the planet Saturn itself at the same frequency. Assume that the thermal emission here takes place in the optically thick regime. Consider that from the disc of the planet Saturn at distance $d = 8$ au we can measure a total monochromatic flux $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{S}} = 2\,900$ Jy. Neglect the shielding of the disc by the rings. The radius of the planet Saturn is $R_{\mathrm{S}} = 58\,232$ km.

h) Determine the brightness temperature $T_{\mathrm{S,b}}$ of Saturn's disc (numerically in K), i.e. the temperature computed on the assumption that all of the observed flux $\Phi_{\nu,\mathrm{S}}$ is of thermal origin. Determine also the expected equilibrium temperature of Saturn's surface $T_{\mathrm{S,e}}$ (computed on the assumption that Saturn has no internal energy sources). Assume Saturn's Bond albedo $A_{\mathrm{B,S}} = 0.35$. Compare the values $T_{\mathrm{S,b}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{S,e}}$ and discuss the origin of any discrepancy. [3.5 points]

F. The Sachs–Wolfe effect

In this problem we shall examine the influence of structures in the Universe on the cosmic microwave background. Specifically, we shall focus on the shift of the wavelengths of CMB photons when passing through the gravitational field of the seeds of large-scale structures in the very early Universe. The consequences of this shift (we speak of the so-called Sachs–Wolfe effect) show up directly as contributions to the anisotropies in the observed CMB temperature – see Figure 4. We shall see that measuring the size of these anisotropies reveals some interesting information about the structure of matter and the laws of physics in the early Universe.

Figure 4: All-sky map of the anisotropies of the temperature of the relic radiation taken by the PLANCK satellite. Red marks regions of higher temperature, blue on the contrary regions of lower temperature. The size of these fluctuations is of the order of $10\ \mu\mathrm{K}$ around the mean value $\bar{T} \approx 2.73$ K.

In general one can say that photons escaping from a gravitational field lose energy – they undergo a gravitational redshift. The wavelength of a photon, during its transfer from a point with gravitational potential $\Phi_0$ to a point with gravitational potential $\Phi$, changes from the value $\lambda_0$ to the value $\lambda$, where the ratio of $\lambda$ and $\lambda_0$ can be obtained from the relation
$$\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0} \approx 1 + \frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{c^2}\,. \qquad (9)$$
We assume $\Phi \ll c^2$. Differences in the value of the gravitational potential also lead to a different perception of time by different observers: if an observer at a place with gravitational potential $\Phi_0$ measures a time interval $\Delta t_0$, then
$$\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta t_0} \approx 1 + \frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{c^2}\,, \qquad (10)$$
where $\Delta t$ is the corresponding time interval measured by an observer at the place with potential $\Phi$.

On large scales the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic with mean density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter (dark and baryonic). On smaller scales we observe inhomogeneities in the distribution of matter. The density $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter can thus in general be written as $\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, where $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ is a deviation that depends on position. To describe the inhomogeneities it is convenient to introduce the dimensionless quantity
$$\delta_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}}{\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}}\,, \qquad (11)$$
which we call the density contrast. In this problem we shall for simplicity model the inhomogeneities as spherical regions of radius $R$ with homogeneous density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}} > \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$, existing within the surrounding homogeneous and isotropic universe of density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$. We shall work exclusively in the so-called linear regime, in which $|\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}| \ll |\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}|$ and hence $\delta_{\mathrm{m}} \ll 1$.

Let us move to a reference frame whose origin is placed at the centre of the spherical region with homogeneous overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$. Denote by $r$ the distance measured from the centre of the region. To find the gravitational potential $\Phi(r)$ caused by the spherical overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ we can use the fact that, for a spherical mass distribution, only the mass located at radii smaller than $r$ contributes to the gravitational force acting on a test body placed at radius $r$. This mass then behaves as if it were compressed into a point mass placed at the origin. Moreover, the potential $\Phi(r)$ and the corresponding gravitational force must be continuous functions for all $r$.

Using this information we could derive that outside the spherical region of overdensity (i.e. for $r > R$) the potential $\Phi(r)$ can be written as
$$\Phi(r) = -\frac{4}{3}\pi G R^2 \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}\delta_{\mathrm{m}}\frac{R}{r}\,, \qquad (r > R) \qquad (12)$$
while inside the region of overdensity (for $r \leqslant R$) we would obtain for the potential
$$\Phi(r) = 2\pi G R^2 \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}\delta_{\mathrm{m}}\left(\frac{r^2}{3R^2} - 1\right). \qquad (r \leqslant R) \qquad (13)$$

a) Write the relation for the depth $\Delta\Phi = \Phi(\infty) - \Phi(0)$ of the potential well generated by a homogeneous spherical overdensity (express it in terms of $G$, $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$, $R$). [1.5 points]

b) Sketch the graph of the potential $\Phi(r)$ as a function of $r$ for all $r > 0$. In your graph mark clearly the edge $r = R$ of the region of overdensity, the value of the potential at this point, and also the minimum of the gravitational potential (the bottom of the well). [3 points]

Let us now focus on the inhomogeneities that existed in the Universe at the epoch of formation of the CMB, i.e. at the moment of decoupling of the relic radiation from matter. In the following tasks you may assume that our Universe is exactly flat, that the present mean temperature of the CMB is $\bar{T}_0 = 2.73$ K, that the cosmological redshift corresponding to the epoch of CMB formation is $z = 1\,090$, that the present value of the Hubble–Lemaître parameter is $H_0 = 67.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, and that the present fraction of the density of matter in the total density in the Universe is $\Omega_{\mathrm{m},0} = 0.315$.

c) Compute the density $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}}$ of matter in the Universe (numerically in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$) at the epoch of CMB formation. [2.5 points]

Let us now try to analyse the relation between the density fluctuations $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$ at the epoch of CMB formation and the observed temperature anisotropies of the CMB at various angular scales. The observed spectrum of fluctuations (size of the temperature fluctuation as a function of its angular size) can be seen in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Observed spectrum of CMB anisotropies (data from the PLANCK mission). The quantity plotted on the vertical axis can, in a very simplified way, be understood as the square of the size $\delta T$ of the observed temperature fluctuation. On the horizontal axis (on the upper edge of the graph) the angular size of the fluctuations on the sky is plotted.

First, assuming adiabaticity of the perturbations of the expansion of the Universe, we can regard regions of overdensity as bubbles of space-time in which the evolution of the Universe lags slightly behind its surroundings: as if regions with a small overdensity $\delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ were characterised by an "older" scale factor $a - \delta a$ instead of $a$, where the deviation $0 < \delta a \ll 1$ is chosen such that
$$\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m},0}\,(a - \delta a)^{-3}\,,$$
while $\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m}} = \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{m},0}\,a^{-3}$. Since the Universe had a higher temperature at smaller scale factors, we thus obtain a positive contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the difference between the temperature of matter in the region of overdensity and the temperature $\bar{T}$ of matter in the surrounding Universe.

d) Show that one can write the approximate relation
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}}{\bar{T}} \approx \frac{1}{3}\,\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$$
between the adiabatic fluctuation $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ of the CMB temperature, the mean temperature $\bar{T}$ of the relic radiation at the epoch of its formation and the density contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$. You may find it useful that $(1+x)^p \approx 1 + px$ for $x \ll 1$. [2 points]

This, however, is not the only effect contributing to the temperature fluctuations of the CMB: the presence of an overdensity also causes a local slowing of the flow of (cosmological) time due to gravitational time dilation according to relation (10) above. This leads to a further lag in the evolution of the region of overdensity compared with its surroundings, and hence to a further positive contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}}$ to the difference between the temperature of the region of overdensity and its surroundings. In the following tasks consider that the expansion of the Universe at the epoch of CMB formation was dominated by matter, so that $a(t) \propto t^{2/3}$.

e) Show that we can write the approximate relation
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}}}{\bar{T}} \approx \frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\,,$$
where $\Delta\Phi$ is the depth of the gravitational potential well caused by the region of overdensity. [2.5 points]

Finally, an outside observer obtains information about the temperature in the region of overdensity through the photons that escape from it. As already described in the introduction to the problem, these photons undergo a gravitational redshift. The outside observer interprets this as a negative contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{red}}$ to the total temperature fluctuation of the region of overdensity compared with its surroundings.

f) Show that approximately
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{red}}}{\bar{T}} \approx -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}\,.$$
Write also the relation for the total temperature fluctuation $\delta T = \delta T_{\mathrm{ad}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{dil}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{red}}$ due to the presence of the region of overdensity in terms of $\bar{T}$, $G$, $R$, $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $c$. [3.5 points]

The partial contribution
$$\frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}}{\bar{T}} = \frac{\delta T_{\mathrm{dil}} + \delta T_{\mathrm{red}}}{\bar{T}} \approx -\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\Delta\Phi}{c^2}$$
to the temperature fluctuation, which includes all terms explicitly dependent on the radius $R$ of the region of overdensity, is called the ordinary Sachs–Wolfe effect. (In the literature one also meets the so-called integrated Sachs–Wolfe effect, which, however, we shall not deal with in this problem.) From your result in part f) it should be evident that for sufficiently small values of $R$ the resulting temperature fluctuation is dominated by the adiabatic contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$, whereas for large values of $R$ the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect prevails.

g) Determine the critical value $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ of the radius of the region of overdensity at the epoch of CMB formation (numerically in kpc) for which the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the total temperature fluctuation is comparable with the contribution $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect. To what angular radius $\alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$ of the fluctuation would this value correspond on today's sky? Discuss how the value $R_{\mathrm{crit}}$ relates to the radius $c/H$ of the Hubble sphere at the epoch of recombination. [3 points]

Hint: Converting linear distances to angular ones is very complicated for large redshifts: for $z \gg 1$ one can no longer naively use Hubble's law to compute the distance, and details of the expansion model we consider come into play. You may instead use the well-known fact that the so-called sound horizon at the moment of decoupling of the CMB radiation from matter, which has a linear size of 133 kpc, corresponds on today's sky to an angular distance of $0.6^\circ$.

Since the adiabatic contributions $\delta T_{\mathrm{ad}}$ to the temperature fluctuations are given directly by the density contrast $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}$, we can say that the shape of the CMB anisotropy spectrum in Fig. 6 in the regime $\alpha < \alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is a direct imprint of the distribution $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}(R)$ of the density contrast as a function of the size $R$ of the region of overdensity at the epoch of CMB formation. This regime includes, among other things, the so-called acoustic peaks, which we can observe in the right part of the spectrum. On the contrary, the contributions $\delta T_{\mathrm{SW}}$ of the Sachs–Wolfe effect ($\alpha \gg \alpha_{\mathrm{crit}}$) prevail in the extreme left part of the spectrum in Fig. 6, where we observe an approximately constant distribution of $\delta T$ as a function of the angular size $\alpha$ (and hence also of the linear size $R$) of the region of overdensity.

h) What dependence $\delta_{\mathrm{m}}(R)$ of the density contrast on the radius $R$ of the region of overdensity follows from the data in Fig. 6 in the regime $R \gg R_{\mathrm{crit}}$? [2 points]

G. Profile of the Milky Way

The Milky Way reaches its highest declination in the constellation Cassiopeia. Jindra wondered how much higher the density of stars in the Milky Way is compared with other regions of the sky. He therefore looked at a star chart and counted stars brighter than 10 mag in squares on the sky. The squares measure $2^\circ$ of declination by 0 h 15 min of right ascension. Jindra counted stars in squares between 00 h 00 min and 00 h 15 min of right ascension from $42^\circ$ to $72^\circ$ of declination. The star counts are given in Table 1.

a) Compute in steradians the sizes of all 15 regions of the sky in which Jindra counted stars. [5 points]

Hint: The area of a spherical cap of height $h$ is $S = 2\pi Rh$, where $R$ is the radius of the sphere. The whole sphere has a solid angle of $4\pi$ steradians.

b) Compute the star densities (number of stars per unit solid angle) in the 15 regions of the sky and their uncertainties. [5 points]

Hint: For the star counts you may consider Poisson uncertainties $\Delta N = \sqrt{N}$.

c) Plot how the density of stars on the sky changes with declination. Draw the error bars too. [5 points]

d) Write the range of declination angles where, according to the graph, the Milky Way lies, and justify your decision. Compute, by the method of weighted mean, the mean densities of stars brighter than 10 mag in the Milky Way and also outside the Milky Way, and their uncertainties. How much higher is the density of stars in the Milky Way, and what is the uncertainty of this difference? [5 points]

Hint: The weighted mean $\mu$ of data $(x_i, \sigma_i)$, where $x_i$ are the data and $\sigma_i$ are the measurement uncertainties, is
$$\frac{\mu}{\sigma_\mu^2} = \sum_i \frac{x_i}{\sigma_i^2}\,.$$
The uncertainty of the weighted mean $\sigma_\mu$ can be computed from the relation $\dfrac{1}{\sigma_\mu^2} = \sum_i \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i^2}$.

e) Now let us try to estimate the number of stars brighter than 10 mag on the whole sky. Assume that the densities of stars outside the Milky Way and in the Milky Way that you computed in part d) hold over the whole starry sky. Also assume that the Milky Way has the same width over the whole sky, which you can read off the graph from part c). How many stars brighter than 10 mag are there on the whole sky, and what is the uncertainty of the number of stars? [5 points]

H. O–C diagram

Consider a hypothetical eclipsing variable star for which, on the basis of previous observations, a rough estimate of the orbital period $P_0 \approx 0.324$ d has been established. For this variable star there are also indications that its period changes uniformly in time. Astronomers therefore decided to carry out a series of further observations by means of which they could determine both a more precise value $P$ of the orbital period and the possible size $\Delta P$ of its change per orbit.

Let us first outline the method by which we shall determine the values $P$ and $\Delta P$. Suppose that the first observed primary minimum of the series occurred at time $t_{p,0}$.

a) Write the relation for the predicted time $C_n$ of the primary minimum after $n$ orbits have elapsed since the epoch $t_{p,0}$, which we would compute using the initial estimate $P_0$ of the orbital period. Express the result in terms of $t_{p,0}$, $P_0$ and $n$. [1 point]

If, however, the actual period at the epoch $t_{p,0}$ is equal to $P$, and if moreover the size of the period changes during each orbit by a constant value $\Delta P$, we shall in reality observe the primary minima at times $O_n$, which will differ from the computed times $C_n$.

b) Show that we can write [1.5 points]
$$O_n = t_{p,0} + nP + \frac{1}{2}\,n(n+1)\,\Delta P\,. \qquad (1)$$

c) Write the relation for the difference $O_n - C_n$ of the observed times of primary minimum as a function of the number $n$ of orbits that have elapsed since the epoch $t_{p,0}$. Your relation should contain the parameters $P$, $P_0$ and $\Delta P$. [1 point]
